california.lead: California is simply the biggest pool of people within about 2,400–2,700 miles of Hawaiʻi. Per resident, Californians buy at about the same rate as people in Washington, Nevada, Oregon and Utah (30–41 buyers per million in 2025), and five to six times the rate of Texas or Florida. Distance decides who is in range, and income decides who buys within it. That is why the Bay Area and Los Angeles lead.
labels: Size and location: the most populous state within about 2,400–2,700 miles, buying per resident like Washington, Nevada, Oregon and Utah
Visitor familiarity: California sends about 38% of US visitors, and its share of buyers matches
Nonstop flights carry the demand more than they create it
Wealth: within flying range, income decides how many buy and how much they spend
The Bay Area and LA are the two largest pools of nearby high-income households and the two biggest gateways
Family ties: California is Hawaiʻi's largest two-way migration partner
Remote work: a 2021–22 boost, not the reason for the ranking
Time zone: a minor convenience
Taxes are not a driver: from 2027 Hawaiʻi taxes high earners about as heavily as California does
california.brokers: On the neighbor islands most California dollars go to the top of the market, but not all purchases: on Hawaiʻi Island in 2025, 112 of California's 406 purchases were Puna properties averaging about $230K. In 2025, California buyers on the neighbor islands paid on average 2 to 3.6 times what local buyers paid (Maui County 2.0×, Kauaʻi 2.8×, Hawaiʻi Island 3.6×). On Oʻahu they paid close to local prices (about $1.03M against $0.87M), which fits relocation, family and military moves, though that mix cannot be measured. California buyers fell 14% in January–June 2026 while Washington buyers rose 17%.
california.families: California supplied about 38% of mainland buyers in 2008–15 and 37–46% in 2024–26, so that demand will not vanish with a tax change or a rate cycle. On Oʻahu, Californians made about 6% of 2025 purchases. Rules aimed at homes that are not a main residence, such as vacation-rental limits and Honolulu's Residential A tax tiers, reach these buyers far more than income-tax changes do.

west_states.lead: The real pattern is the West against everyone else. By raw count in 2025, Texas (175) and Florida (159) outranked Colorado (136), Oregon (133) and Utah (105); in January–June 2026 Florida (41) fell behind all three. Per resident, though, Alaska, Nevada, Washington, Oregon, Utah and Colorado buy three to more than ten times as often as Texas or Florida. The western states are closer, have more nonstop flights and send far more visitors. Each island pattern has its own reason. Seattle flies nonstop to all four main airports. Alaskans fly Anchorage–Kona in winter and buy where prices are lowest. Colorado and Utah visitors favor Kauaʻi, but their purchases there are few and unstable.
labels: Visitor funnel: western states send far more visitors per resident (a correlation, not proof)
Flight network: Seattle serves all four islands, and Anchorage–Kona flies in winter
Winter escape: strong for Alaska only
Price: Hawaiʻi Island is cheapest, which shapes where Alaskans and Oregonians buy, not whether they buy
Lāʻie and BYU–Hawaiʻi ties explain where some Utah owners are
Family and migration ties: real for Nevada, Washington, Oregon and Alaska
Colorado and Utah on Kauaʻi: clear in visitor data, small and unstable in buyer data
west_states.brokers: Per resident, in 2025 Nevada bought 41 Hawaiʻi homes per million residents, Washington 35, Oregon 31 and Utah 30, against about 6 for Texas and 7 for Florida. Within the West, visitor rates do not predict which state buys more. Colorado's 2025 Kauaʻi spike came largely from 12 Hanalei purchases averaging about $460K in one half-year, so it may not repeat.
west_states.families: On Hawaiʻi Island, buyers from Alaska, Oregon and Washington are mostly not luxury buyers, and some compete directly with local families for cheap Puna lots and starter homes. On Kauaʻi, Utah buyers are mostly in Poʻipū and Princeville and paid about $1.9M on average in 2025, well above local budgets; Colorado buyers averaged about $1.1M, close to the $1.0M local-buyer average.

japan_korea.lead: Japan's ties to Hawaiʻi run through Honolulu. Every flight from Japan lands there, 98% of Japanese visitors spend time on Oʻahu, and owners with Japan mailing addresses already hold about 2,000 Oʻahu parcels, nearly all condos. The 2026 rise in buyers from Japan despite a weak yen is mostly one tower. The Park Ward Village closed 527 pre-sold units in Q2 2026, on contracts signed in 2021–22 when the yen was ¥112–123 to the dollar. Outside that building, purchases by buyers with Japan addresses fell to about 72 on Oʻahu, from 84 a year earlier. Purchases by buyers with Korea addresses jumped the same way, when Victoria Place (late 2024) and The Park on Keʻeaumoku (late 2025) closed.
labels: Tower closings: pre-sold contracts are recorded only when the building delivers
Links only to Oʻahu: flights, repeat visits and an existing base of Japanese condo owners
Developers market Honolulu towers in Tokyo
Wealth and diversification out of the yen and won helped buyers close; they did not add new buying
Home-country rules: Korea's 2020 multi-home taxes came just before the Korean pre-sale wave
Flight capacity explains where they buy, not when
The weak yen is a drag on new contracts, not a cause of the 2026 rise
japan_korea.brokers: Counts of buyers with Japan or Korea addresses track tower delivery schedules more than the exchange rate: Oʻahu recorded only 32 Japan-address purchases in Q1 2026, before the tower closed. With the yen near ¥158, new contracts from Japan are likely to stay soft.
japan_korea.families: Buyers with Japan or Korea addresses made about 2.6% of Oʻahu purchases in 2025 (289 of 11,097). They bought mostly new Kakaʻako and Ala Moana tower units and Waikīkī resort condos, priced well above the Oʻahu condo median, so most local condo shoppers aren't bidding against them. Where they matter is specific buildings, where part-time occupancy runs high.

canada.lead: Canadians lead foreign buying by number of sales on Maui and Hawaiʻi Island because Japan's much larger buyer base stays on Oʻahu, while Canada's winter visitors lean toward Maui and Kona. The 2025 drop, from 106 to 64 purchases, happened on the neighbor islands, mostly among South Maui buyers (33 to 6). Two shocks fit the data. First, a South Maui condo slump hit every buyer group as the vacation-rental phase-out loomed. Second, Canadians broadly pulled back from US travel and property after the November 2024 tariff threat.
labels: A Western-Canada winter corridor to Maui and Kona, with an existing base of owners with Canada addresses
Seasonality shapes when Canadians buy, not how many
The 2025 political shock: a pullback from US travel and property
The weak Canadian dollar: background, not the 2025 cause
Maui's condo slump and the threat of the Bill 9 phase-out
Fewer flights from Canada, mostly a result of weaker demand
US tax rules shape how Canadians own homes; they did not cause the drop
canada.brokers: closings by buyers from Canada on the neighbor islands have run at 11 to 18 per half-year since early 2025 (18 in January–June 2025, 11 in July–December 2025, 18 in January–June 2026), with no sign yet of a rebound. About 1,600 Maui County properties send their tax bills to Canada, many of them South Maui condos; only the apartment-zoned (Minatoya-list) units among them face the Bill 9 phase-out, and their number is not known.
canada.families: Canadians are a small share of island buying today: 11 of 1,247 Maui County sales and 17 of 3,675 Hawaiʻi Island sales in 2025. Their retreat matters mainly in South Maui. Canadian visits held up far better than buying from Canada in 2025 (Canadian visitors to Maui −4.4%, purchases by buyers from Canada in Maui County −72%), though Canadian visitors statewide fell 12.7%.

maui_decline.lead: Most of Maui's fall from about 52% mainland buyers in 2010 to 25% in 2025 is not a mainland exodus. First, 2010 was an abnormal starting year, full of bust-era resort-condo closings. Second, in Q3 2018 the published series broke. Title Guaranty's Maui condo count dropped to about 75% of MLS condo sales, and the mainland share stepped down from 39% to 29% in a single quarter. County tax records over the same period show buyers without a homeowner exemption steady at 55–56% (FY2018–FY2020). Third, after the 2021–22 surge, outside buying fell faster than local buying, but in county tax records the share of buyers without a homeowner exemption only returned to its pre-pandemic level (57% in FY2025, against 54–57% in FY2016–20).
labels: A 2018 break in the published series, concentrated in condos (cause unconfirmed)
An abnormal 2010 starting point
A real post-2021 pullback by outside buyers, back to pre-pandemic levels
Vacation-rental policy risk (Bill 9), visible in South Maui
The Lahaina fire: fewer deals, not a lower outside share
Condo insurance and HOA costs: a minor factor
A fixed supply of resort condos: no evidence it matters
maui_decline.brokers: The 25% figure understates outside demand: in county conveyance-tax records, buyers without a homeowner exemption were still about 57% of Maui home purchases in FY2025–26, and UHERO counts 55–59% of condo buyers as out-of-state. Maui buyer origin reads best with Title Guaranty, MLS and conveyance-tax data side by side.
maui_decline.families: Competition from buyers without a homeowner exemption (a mix of second-home buyers, investors and local landlords) has returned to its pre-pandemic level; it has not faded. The opening is in apartment-zoned (Minatoya-list) condos whose rental future is in doubt. Prices there have fallen, but check the association's insurance, reserves and special assessments before buying.

investors_military.lead: Investor buying follows where vacation renting happens, not the island line. Across 47 ZIPs, the share of homes used as short-term rentals explains nearly two-thirds of the variation in investor loans. In resort areas 29–54% of loans go to investors, against 3–12% in non-resort towns such as Kahului, Wailuku, Kalāheo, Mililani, ʻEwa and Waipahu. The exceptions are Puna and Hilo on Hawaiʻi Island (19–48%) and Ala Moana–Ward on Oʻahu (30%). VA loans are 27% of Oʻahu purchase loans because about 43,700 active-duty members and 44,100 dependents live there. With no down payment, no mortgage insurance and lower rates, VA is their cheapest way to buy.
labels: Where vacation rentals operate (an association, not proof)
Oʻahu's military population
VA loan terms: the cheapest way to buy for those eligible
Military rotations and housing allowances keep VA buyers coming
How lenders label loans: vacation homes recoded from 'second home' to 'investment'
Long-term rents rarely cover a financed payment, except in Puna
Oʻahu's 90-day rental minimum is not the reason
Loan limits are the same on every island
investors_military.brokers: VA loans made up 36–44% of mortgaged purchases in the ʻEwa, Waiʻanae and Wahiawā subdivisions in 2025. Long-term rents rarely cover a financed payment except in Puna, so investor buying tracks where vacation renting happens.
investors_military.families: On Oʻahu, non-military families compete with buyers who can put zero down and borrow at about half a point less, most of all in the ʻEwa, Waiʻanae and Wahiawā areas. On Maui and Kauaʻi, investor competition is concentrated in resort areas; on Hawaiʻi Island it is just as heavy in Puna and Hilo. State and county first-time-buyer programs can help close the down-payment gap.

affordability.lead: Two shocks hit in sequence. First, prices jumped in 2020–22, mostly while rates were near 3% (2020–21) and listings had nearly vanished. Then mortgage rates averaged 6.6% in 2025, up from 3.9% in 2019, which raised the payment on every borrowed dollar by 35%, and prices did not fall back. On Oʻahu the two pushed about equally: each added 14–24 points, depending on which is counted first. On Maui and Kauaʻi prices pushed harder, adding 30–41 points against 13–25 for rates. Rising incomes took back part of it. Hawaiʻi's chronic limits explain why the starting point was already about 40%: slow permits, little urban land and high building costs.
labels: The 2020–22 price run-up: the largest piece
Mortgage rates: about as big as prices on Oʻahu, and nearly all of the rise since 2021
Income growth took some of it back
Chronic supply limits: why it started high and didn't fall
Construction costs: a modest, indirect push
Outside buyers: behind neighbor-island price levels and the 2021–22 spike
Vacation rentals and second homes raise Maui and Kauaʻi price levels
Condo insurance and dues are not in the headline figure, and add 6–10 points of income for an Oʻahu condo buyer
affordability.brokers: Each point of mortgage rate moves the payment about 10–11%. At the October 8 rate of 7.40%, the report's formula, using 2026-to-date median prices and 2024 incomes, gives about 75% of income on Oʻahu, 82% on Maui and 89% on Kauaʻi. Condo insurance, reserves and special assessments now affect whether a condo purchase can be financed.
affordability.families: The headline figure compares one median house with one median household. It leaves out taxes, insurance and condo dues, so treat it as a gauge, not a budget. Rates matter most now: a one-point drop is worth roughly a 10% price cut. But prices also rose faster than pay in 2020–22, so lower rates alone won't bring back 2019 conditions. The lasting fix is more housing, which depends on permit speed and zoning.

leavers.lead: Departing households leave mainly because of housing costs. They land where housing is cheaper and jobs have grown, the same pull that draws movers from every state. In August 2026 a typical Honolulu asking rent (Zillow Observed Rent Index) was about $1,300 a month above Las Vegas or Phoenix. Las Vegas is the one place Hawaiʻi residents favor far more than other Americans do. About 1,650 households a year went there in 2019–23 (IRS data), roughly 2.4 for every one that came back. Military orders are a separate channel, and taxes matter little.
labels: The housing-cost gap
Las Vegas, the 'ninth island': community, decades of casino marketing and frequent flights
Military orders: about 9% of Oʻahu's leavers go to base-dominated counties, about 18% counting Tacoma, San Antonio and El Paso
Jobs: leavers follow the same job growth as other Americans
Family and community networks: real for Las Vegas and Utah County
State income tax: about $1,600–3,400 a year, small next to housing costs
leavers.brokers: Las Vegas is the only strongly one-way corridor. Base-town flows (San Antonio, El Paso, Colorado Springs, Tacoma, San Diego) follow military orders. Flows to Denver and Salt Lake City are smaller (about 180–360 households a year) and run both ways. The housing payment gap, not taxes, is the larger cost difference.
leavers.families: The flow to Las Vegas fell 38% from its 2006–07 peak to 2009–10 (IRS years), as Nevada's economy collapsed: the cheapest destinations can have volatile job markets. Coming back is hard once Hawaiʻi prices move on. If you might return, weigh renting out your home instead of selling it. You would lose the homeowner exemption, and renting it out for more than three years would also cost you the federal capital-gains exclusion on a later sale, so get tax advice first.

extra_sources.source: Zillow Observed Rent Index, metro, August 2026 (retrieved 2026-10-08)

now_2026.lead: The turn toward buyers is real, but narrower and later than the headlines suggest. Oʻahu's +9% recorded sales in the first half came from one tower. The Park Ward Village closed 527 pre-sold units in Q2 2026; without it, Oʻahu's recorded sales fell about 2% and MLS resales were flat. Kauaʻi's −34% is measured against an odd batch of about 80 cheap Līhuʻe condo transfers in Q2 2025; adjusted for those, the drop is about 18–21%. Rates drive the late-2026 cooling: the 30-year rate rose from a 6.05% February average to 7.40% on October 8.
labels: Recorded deeds vs MLS resales: one-time closings distort the headline
Two markets: scarce Oʻahu houses, oversupplied condos
Fewer buyers on Kauaʻi and Hawaiʻi Island, concentrated in Kauaʻi condos
Mortgage rates drive the late-2026 cooling
Maui has been a buyer's market since 2024 and is now clearing
Tourism explains little
Buyers from Canada and Japan are too few to move island markets
Data quirks: Realtor.com quality flags and different months-of-supply definitions
now_2026.brokers: Recorded sales and MLS resales measure different things, and developer closings move the recorded count. Oʻahu houses remain tight (about 3 months of supply, 17 days on market), while Oʻahu and Maui condos are the looser segment, where dues, insurance and assessments weigh on deals. Maui's board data and Realtor.com's flagged data give different months of supply.
now_2026.families: Oʻahu house buyers get little relief. House listings are 27% below 2019, and the rate rise since February means the same payment buys about 13% less house. Condo and neighbor-island buyers have real leverage, but HOA fees, insurance deductibles and special assessments can cancel out a price discount.

micro_hotspots.lead: On Oʻahu, off-island owners cluster in specific buildings and plats, not whole neighborhoods. Hotel-and-resort-class condos are about 52% owned off-island. Kuilima/Turtle Bay is about half off-island, against 2–5% in Kahuku town, and Kahuku ranks second on the ZIP list, behind Waikīkī, only because Turtle Bay is about half of a tiny ZIP. Neighbor-island luxury sits where luxury was built: by a brokerage's map counts, South Kohala and North Kona, home to the resort and club communities, took about 86% of Hawaiʻi Island's $3M+ house sales in 2025, and West and South Maui took 82% of Maui's. Kahala is the exception: an older enclave of large lots where short-stay rentals are barred and buyers below roughly $5–10M are mostly local.
labels: Where visitor rentals are legal or grandfathered (an association, not proof)
Condos and condotels: lock-and-leave units
Master-planned resort and club communities
Kahala: older wealth, large lots, no short-stay rentals
Dry, sunny coasts helped site the resorts but aren't required
West Coast wealth explains why buyers come, not where they buy
Koʻolauloa community ties: Utah-linked owners in Lāʻie and Hauʻula
micro_hotspots.brokers: Off-island ownership concentrates by building and plat, not ZIP: Waikīkī hotel-condos, Kuilima, Ko Olina, Mākaha, Punaluʻu and Kakaʻako towers. Kahuku town, Lāʻie and Hauʻula houses, and the wider Kahala–Kaimukī ZIP are 85–98% locally owned. The exception is the $10M+ tier: most Oʻahu homes at that level have no homeowner exemption and are often held by entities.
micro_hotspots.families: Most homes, even in these ZIPs, are locally owned. Off-island competition is sharpest for older condos in Waikīkī and Punaluʻu, which are often a family's first purchase; in Hauʻula, mainland buyers in 2023–25 paid a median of about $439K (28 sales). Where rules stop visitor renting, off-island demand should cool.
